text: But I am poor and needy: make haste unto me, O God: thou art my help and my deliverer; O LORD, make no tarrying.
reflection: David prays with raw honesty: "But I am poor and needy: make haste unto me, O God: thou art my help and my deliverer; O LORD, make no tarrying." David was a king, yet he described himself as poor and needy. He knew that, before God, every person stands in need. This humility is the root of compassion. When we recognize our own neediness, we become more tender toward others who are struggling. We stop seeing the poor as different from us. We are all dependent on God's help. As we begin this month focused on service and compassion, let this prayer shape your heart. First, bring your own needs honestly to God. He is your help and deliverer. Then look around with new eyes. Who near you is poor and needy, whether in money, health, friendship, or hope? Let the compassion God shows you flow toward them. Be an answer to someone else's prayer for help today.
question: Who near you is poor and needy, in money, health, friendship, or hope, and how could you help?
prayer: Lord, I am poor and needy before You, and You are my help and my deliverer. Let the compassion You show me flow toward someone in need today. Amen.

text: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
reflection: Paul gives a short, practical command that could transform every relationship: "And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you." Kindness, tenderness, and forgiveness. These are not optional extras for nice people. They are the natural response of those who have been forgiven by God. Notice the measure: even as God has forgiven you. God's forgiveness toward us is generous, complete, and undeserved. And that becomes the pattern for how we forgive others. Forgiveness is not pretending the hurt did not happen. It is choosing to release the debt, just as God released ours. It is often a process, not a single moment. But it brings freedom, both to the one forgiven and to the one forgiving. Today, think of someone you need to forgive. It may be someone close or someone from long ago. Ask God for a tender heart. Remember how much you have been forgiven, and take a step toward releasing them.
question: Whom do you need to forgive, and how can remembering God's forgiveness help you take a step toward it?
prayer: Lord, You have forgiven me so much for Christ's sake. Make me kind and tenderhearted, and help me take a step toward forgiving the one who hurt me. Amen.

text: But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me: thou art my help and my deliverer; make no tarrying, O my God.
reflection: Here is another prayer of David that begins the same way: "But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me." That middle phrase is one of the most comforting in the Bible. The Lord thinks upon me. The God who holds the universe has you on His mind. You are not forgotten, overlooked, or lost in the crowd. Even when you feel poor and needy, He is thinking of you with care. And because God thinks upon the needy, His people should too. Compassion begins with noticing. It means keeping people in mind, remembering their struggles, and checking in on them. Many people feel invisible. They wonder if anyone thinks of them at all. You can be a reflection of God's attention. Today, rest in the truth that God is thinking of you. Then think of someone else who may feel forgotten. Send a message, make a call, or say a prayer. Let them know they are on your mind, and on God's.
question: Who may feel forgotten that you could let know they are on your mind today?
prayer: Lord, I am poor and needy, yet You think upon me. Thank You for never forgetting me. Help me remember someone who feels forgotten today. Amen.

text: Jesus said unto him, If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me.
reflection: A wealthy young man asked Jesus what he still lacked. Jesus looked at him with love and said, "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me." The young man went away sorrowful, because he had great possessions. Jesus was not giving a universal rule that every believer must sell everything. He was addressing what held this man's heart. His wealth had become a rival to God. And the remedy was generosity toward the poor and wholehearted following of Jesus. This encounter invites us to ask: what holds my heart? What would be hardest to let go of? Jesus does not ask for our possessions because He is stingy. He asks because He wants to free us and give us treasure that lasts. Today, find one way to give generously to someone in need. Let your giving loosen the grip of possessions and draw you closer to following Jesus.
question: What possession has a grip on your heart, and how could giving loosen it?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You want my whole heart. Loosen the grip my possessions have on me, make me generous to those in need, and help me follow You. Amen.

text: But Martha was cumbered about much serving, and came to him, and said, Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me.
reflection: Martha had opened her home to Jesus and was working hard to serve. Meanwhile, her sister Mary sat at His feet, listening. Frustrated, Martha said, "Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me." Luke says she was cumbered about much serving, distracted and weighed down. Jesus gently replied that Mary had chosen the better part. Martha's service was good, but it had become anxious and resentful. She was so busy serving Jesus that she had no time to be with Him. Many of us know how Martha felt. We serve our families, churches, and communities, and sometimes we feel unappreciated and overwhelmed. Jesus does not condemn our service. He invites us to begin where Mary began, at His feet. Service that flows from time with Him is joyful rather than resentful. Today, before you serve, sit with Jesus. Let Him fill your heart. Then serve from that fullness with a willing spirit.
question: Is your service flowing from time at Jesus' feet, or has it become anxious and resentful?
prayer: Lord Jesus, before I serve, let me sit at Your feet. Fill my heart with Your presence, so that I serve from fullness and joy rather than worry and resentment. Amen.

text: Why was not this ointment sold for three hundred pence, and given to the poor?
reflection: Mary poured expensive perfume on the feet of Jesus, an act of extravagant love. Judas objected: "Why was not this ointment sold for three hundred pence, and given to the poor?" It sounded compassionate. But John tells us the truth in the next verse: Judas did not care for the poor. He was a thief who stole from the money bag. His concern was a mask for his own greed. This is a sobering reminder that compassion can be faked. It is possible to use the language of caring while our hearts are far from it. True compassion is not about appearing generous or criticizing how others give. It is a sincere love that acts quietly for the good of others. Jesus defended Mary, whose love was genuine. Today, examine your own heart. Is your compassion sincere? Do you care for others, or for how you look? Ask God to purify your motives. Then show real compassion to someone in need, without seeking credit.
question: Is your compassion sincere, or is it sometimes about how you look to others?
prayer: Lord, search my heart and purify my motives. Let my compassion be real, and help me care for those in need without seeking credit. Amen.

text: (As it is written, He hath dispersed abroad; he hath given to the poor: his righteousness remaineth for ever.
reflection: Paul quotes a psalm about the generous person: "He hath dispersed abroad; he hath given to the poor: his righteousness remaineth for ever." Generosity toward the poor is described as righteousness, living rightly before God. And it is lasting. What we give to those in need is not lost. It has eternal value. Paul was encouraging the Corinthians to give generously to believers in need. He reminded them that God loves a cheerful giver and is able to supply all they need so they can abound in every good work. Generosity is not about how much we have. It is about a heart that freely shares with others. And this righteousness is a response to the righteousness God has given us. Having been made right with God through Christ, we are called to live rightly, which includes caring for the poor. Today, scatter some goodness. Give to someone in need, whether with money, time, or a practical gift. Your generosity has eternal significance.
question: How could you scatter some goodness to someone in need today?
prayer: Lord, You are able to make all grace abound. Make me a cheerful and generous giver, scattering goodness to those in need, knowing what I give is never lost. Amen.

text: For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.
reflection: Jesus summed up His entire mission in one sentence: "For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many." The disciples had been arguing about who would be greatest. They wanted positions of power and honor. Jesus turned their thinking upside down. The greatest is the one who serves. And He Himself is the supreme example. The Son of God, who deserved to be served by all creation, came to serve instead. He washed feet, healed the sick, fed the hungry, and finally gave His life. This is the pattern for every follower of Jesus. Greatness in God's kingdom is measured not by how many serve you, but by how many you serve. It is not always glamorous. Often it is quiet and unseen. But it is the way of Jesus. Today, look for a way to serve without seeking recognition. Follow the One who came not to be served, but to serve.
question: Where could you serve today without seeking recognition?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You came not to be served but to serve and to give Your life for many. Make me a servant like You, content to serve quietly and unseen. Amen.

text: And it was given unto him to make war with the saints, and to overcome them: and power was given him over all kindreds, and tongues, and nations.
reflection: Revelation gives a sober picture of evil's power: "And it was given unto him to make war with the saints, and to overcome them: and power was given him over all kindreds, and tongues, and nations." For a time, the beast appears to win. God's people suffer and lose much. Yet a few verses later John adds, "Here is the patience and the faith of the saints." What could the beast take? Possessions, freedom, even life. But it could not take what the saints had already given to God. Their hearts belonged to the Lamb. This is the deepest kind of generosity: giving ourselves to God so completely that nothing in this world can truly rob us. Treasures held tightly can be taken. Lives freely offered to God are kept safe forever. Today, consider what you are clinging to. Hold earthly things loosely. Give them, and yourself, generously to God. What is placed in His hands can never be lost, no matter what powers rise in this world.
question: What earthly thing are you clinging to that you could place in God's hands?
prayer: Lord, nothing placed in Your hands can ever be lost. Help me hold earthly things loosely and give myself, and all I have, generously to You. Amen.

text: For this ointment might have been sold for much, and given to the poor.
reflection: Matthew tells the story of the anointing from a different angle. When a woman poured precious ointment on the head of Jesus, the disciples were indignant: "For this ointment might have been sold for much, and given to the poor." Their concern sounded practical and caring. But Jesus saw something they missed. This woman had done a beautiful thing. She was preparing Him for His burial. Her act of worship was precious to Him, and He said it would be remembered wherever the gospel is preached. This story shows that worship and compassion are not rivals. Jesus cared deeply for the poor, and He also received extravagant love. The disciples saw only a budget line. Jesus saw a heart poured out in devotion. Sometimes we can be so focused on efficiency that we miss moments of beauty. Today, let your love for Jesus be wholehearted. And let that same love overflow into practical care for the poor. Both worship and service honor Him.
question: What wholehearted act of love for Jesus could you offer today, in worship or in service?
prayer: Lord Jesus, let my love for You be wholehearted, not measured. Receive my worship, and let it overflow into practical care for the poor. Amen.

text: For some of them thought, because Judas had the bag, that Jesus had said unto him, Buy those things that we have need of against the feast; or, that he should give something to the poor.
reflection: At the Last Supper, Jesus told Judas to do what he was going to do quickly. The other disciples did not understand. They assumed something ordinary: "some of them thought … that he should give something to the poor." That is remarkable. Giving to the poor was such a normal part of life with Jesus that the disciples assumed it even at the Passover meal. Jesus and His followers regularly set aside money to help those in need. Compassion was woven into their daily rhythm, not reserved for special occasions. This little detail shows us something about the heart of Jesus. Care for the poor was not an afterthought. It was a habit. What if compassion were that natural in our lives too? What if people who knew us assumed that we were always looking for ways to help? Today, consider building a habit of generosity. Set aside something regularly for those in need. Let compassion become so normal in your life that it is simply who you are.
question: What habit of generosity could you build so that compassion becomes part of who you are?
prayer: Lord, let compassion be woven into my everyday life as it was for You and Your disciples. Help me set aside something regularly for those in need. Amen.

text: When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue faileth for thirst, I the LORD will hear them, I the God of Israel will not forsake them.
reflection: God makes a tender promise through Isaiah: "When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue faileth for thirst, I the LORD will hear them, I the God of Israel will not forsake them." Picture someone desperately searching for water and finding none. Their strength is fading. It is a picture of utter need. And into that need, God speaks: I will hear them. I will not forsake them. In the next verses, He promises to open rivers in high places and fountains in the valleys, turning the wilderness into a pool of water. God sees the thirsty, both those who thirst physically and those who thirst spiritually. He does not ignore their cry. And He often answers through His people. Many in our world still lack clean water, food, and basic necessities. Others thirst for hope and love. Today, ask God how you can be part of His answer. Support someone in need, or share the living water of His love.
question: How could you be part of God's answer for someone who is thirsty for water, hope, or love?
prayer: Lord, You hear the poor and needy, and You will not forsake them. Show me how to be part of Your answer for someone who is thirsty today. Amen.

text: But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
reflection: After a long chapter about the resurrection, Paul erupts in thanksgiving: "But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." Victory over sin and death is not something we earn. It is something God gives. He is the generous Giver. Through Jesus, He has given us the greatest gift imaginable: victory over the grave and eternal life. Gratitude for this gift should shape everything about us, including how we give. When we realize how generously God has given to us, our own hearts open wide. Generosity becomes a natural response to grace. We give not to earn God's favor but because we have already received far more than we could ever repay. Today, take a moment to thank God for the victory He has given you. Then let that gratitude overflow. Give something to someone today, a gift, a kind word, an act of service, as an expression of thanks to the God who gives us the victory.
question: How can your thanks for the victory God has given you overflow into giving today?
prayer: Thanks be to You, O God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Let my gratitude overflow in generous giving to someone today. Amen.

text: For it might have been sold for more than three hundred pence, and have been given to the poor. And they murmured against her.
reflection: Mark adds a painful detail to the story of the anointing. After some complained that the ointment "might have been sold for more than three hundred pence, and have been given to the poor," Mark writes, "And they murmured against her." They grumbled and criticized the woman who had just done something beautiful for Jesus. But Jesus defended her. He said, "ye have the poor with you always, and whensoever ye will ye may do them good." He was not dismissing the poor. He was reminding them that care for the poor is an ongoing calling, one they could act on any time they chose. It was not a reason to tear down someone else's devotion. It is easy to criticize how others express their love for God. We may judge their giving, their worship, or their service. But Jesus invites us to focus on our own hearts instead. Today, rather than murmuring about others, do good to someone in need. Let your compassion be action, not criticism.
question: Whose worship or service have you been tempted to criticize, and what good could you do instead?
prayer: Lord Jesus, keep me from murmuring against others. Help me focus on my own heart, and turn my criticism into compassionate action for someone in need. Amen.

text: For what is it wherein ye were inferior to other churches, except it be that I myself was not burdensome to you? forgive me this wrong.
reflection: Paul uses gentle irony with the Corinthians. Some had criticized him, perhaps because he refused to accept financial support from them. So he writes, "For what is it wherein ye were inferior to other churches, except it be that I myself was not burdensome to you? forgive me this wrong." Of course, it was not really a wrong. Paul had worked with his own hands so that he would not be a financial burden to them. He served them freely, out of love. And when that love was misunderstood, he did not respond with bitterness. He responded with humble humor and a request for forgiveness. Sometimes our kindness is misunderstood. We give and are criticized. We serve and are not appreciated. Paul shows us how to respond with grace rather than resentment. Today, if someone has misunderstood your good intentions, let it go. Choose humility over defensiveness. Keep serving with love, and leave the outcome in God's hands.
question: Has someone misunderstood your good intentions, and can you let it go with humility?
prayer: Lord, when my service is misunderstood, keep me from defensiveness. Help me keep serving with love and leave the outcome in Your hands. Amen.

text: For he shall deliver the needy when he crieth; the poor also, and him that hath no helper.
reflection: Psalm 72 is a prayer for the king, describing what a righteous ruler looks like. And at its heart is compassion: "For he shall deliver the needy when he crieth; the poor also, and him that hath no helper." A good king hears the cry of the needy. He rescues the poor. He becomes a helper for those who have no one else. This psalm ultimately points to Jesus, the perfect King, whose reign is marked by care for the lowly. He did not spend His time courting the powerful. He touched lepers, welcomed outcasts, and lifted the downtrodden. And He calls His people to reflect His kingdom. Who around you has no helper? Perhaps an elderly neighbor, a struggling single parent, a refugee family, or a lonely coworker. These are the people Jesus notices. Today, ask God to open your eyes to someone who has no helper. Then step in. Be a reflection of the compassionate King who delivers the needy when they cry.
question: Who around you has no helper, and how could you step in today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, compassionate King, You deliver the needy who cry out. Open my eyes to someone who has no helper, and make me a reflection of Your care. Amen.

text: And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord; Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.
reflection: Zacchaeus was a wealthy tax collector, despised by his community for cheating people. But when Jesus came to his home, everything changed. He stood and said, "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." No one forced him. His generosity flowed from an encounter with Jesus. Grace had found him, and grace made him generous. Jesus responded, "This day is salvation come to this house." There is a deep peace in this story. For years, Zacchaeus had been restless, chasing wealth and living with guilt. Now, in the presence of Jesus, he was free. He could let go of what he had clung to. When we encounter Jesus, our grip on possessions loosens. We find rest not in what we have but in whom we know. Today, rest in His presence. And let His grace make you generous, especially toward those you may have wronged.
question: How has God's grace made you generous, and is there anyone you need to make things right with?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You came to my house as You came to Zacchaeus. Let Your grace loosen my grip on what I have, and make me generous and quick to make things right. Amen.

text: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear…
reflection: Peter writes to believers facing opposition, and he gives them guidance for how to respond: "But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear." First, set apart Christ as Lord in your heart. Let Him be the center. Then be ready to explain your hope when someone asks. Notice that people will ask about your hope. When you live with peace and hope in difficult circumstances, people notice. They wonder how you can stay steady. That is your opportunity to share. And Peter says to do it with meekness and respect, never arrogance or argument. Sharing your faith is not about winning debates. It is about gently explaining why you have hope. Today, think about how you would explain your hope to a friend. Keep it simple and honest. Then pray for an opportunity, and be ready to share it with gentleness.
question: How would you simply and honestly explain your hope to a friend who asked?
prayer: Lord, be set apart as holy in my heart. Make me ready to give a reason for the hope that is in me, with gentleness and respect. Amen.

text: I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. So then with the mind I myself serve the law of God; but with the flesh the law of sin.
reflection: In Romans 7, Paul describes a struggle many of us know well. He wants to do what is right, but he often finds himself doing what he does not want to do. Then comes the turning point: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. So then with the mind I myself serve the law of God; but with the flesh the law of sin." Paul does not pretend the struggle is over. But he knows where deliverance comes from. Thank God through Jesus Christ. The answer is not trying harder; it is trusting Christ. And even in the struggle, Paul's mind is set on serving God. This is honest, hopeful service. We do not serve God perfectly. Our hearts are divided at times. But Jesus has set us free, and our deepest desire is to serve Him. Today, if you are frustrated by your own weakness, do not give up. Thank God for Jesus. Keep serving Him with a willing heart, even while He continues His work in you.
question: Where are you frustrated by your own weakness, and how can you thank God for Jesus in it?
prayer: I thank You, God, through Jesus Christ my Lord. When I am frustrated by my weakness, help me keep serving You with a willing heart while You keep working in me. Amen.

text: Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.
reflection: Matthew records the same powerful words Mark did: "Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many." In Matthew, these words follow a request from the mother of James and John. She asked that her sons sit at the right and left of Jesus in His kingdom. She wanted honor and position for them. Jesus responded by pointing to Himself as the model. Greatness is not about sitting on thrones; it is about serving. It is natural to want the best for those we love, including recognition and success. But Jesus invites us to want something better for them: hearts that serve. The highest honor in His kingdom belongs to those who give themselves for others. Today, if you are a parent, mentor, or friend, encourage those you love toward service rather than status. And model it yourself. Serve someone today in the spirit of Jesus, who gave everything.
question: How could you encourage someone you love toward service rather than status today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, greatness in Your kingdom is found in serving. Help me model that for the people I love, and serve someone today in Your spirit. Amen.

text: And this is the record, that God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
reflection: John states the heart of the gospel simply: "And this is the record, that God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son." God has given. Eternal life is not something we earn or purchase. It is a gift from a generous God. And it is found in a Person, His Son Jesus. To have Jesus is to have life. This verse reveals the generosity of God's heart. He did not hold back His most precious gift. He gave His Son so that we could have life that never ends. Every act of human generosity is a small echo of this great giving. When we give to others, we reflect the character of the God who gave everything. Today, receive this gift with gratitude. Thank God for eternal life in His Son. Then let His generosity inspire you. Give freely to someone today, not because you must, but because you have been given so much. Let your giving honor the God who gave His Son.
question: How does God's gift of His Son inspire you to give freely today?
prayer: Father, You have given me eternal life in Your Son. Thank You for not holding back Your most precious gift. Let Your generosity make me generous today. Amen.

text: And the Lord shall deliver me from every evil work, and will preserve me unto his heavenly kingdom: to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.
reflection: Near the end of his life, Paul had been abandoned by many friends. He was in prison, facing death. Yet he wrote with confidence: "And the Lord shall deliver me from every evil work, and will preserve me unto his heavenly kingdom: to whom be glory for ever and ever." Paul had served faithfully for decades. Now, as his service drew to a close, he trusted God to carry him home. His confidence was not in his own record but in the Lord who preserves. This is an encouragement for anyone who serves faithfully, especially those who feel weary or unappreciated. Your service is not in vain. The Lord sees it, and He will preserve you. Even when others abandon you, He will not. Paul's final focus was on God's glory. His service was never about himself. Today, keep serving with a willing heart, trusting God with your future. Let your life, like Paul's, end in praise: to Him be glory for ever and ever.
question: What future concern can you trust to the Lord while you keep serving faithfully?
prayer: Lord, You will deliver me from every evil work and preserve me for Your heavenly kingdom. I trust You with my future. To You be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

text: Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.
reflection: These words come from a mother's advice to her son, a young king named Lemuel: "Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy." She wanted him to use his voice and position to defend the vulnerable. Those with influence have a responsibility to speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves. This is part of what it means to live righteously. Having been made right with God, we are called to do right in the world. And that includes advocacy for the poor and needy. You may not be a king, but you have a voice. You can speak up when you see injustice. You can support those who are overlooked. You can advocate for fair treatment in your workplace, school, or community. Silence in the face of injustice is not neutral. Today, ask God to show you where your voice is needed. Open your mouth for those who need someone to plead their cause.
question: Where is your voice needed to speak up for someone who cannot speak for themselves?
prayer: Lord, show me where my voice is needed. Give me courage to open my mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy. Amen.

text: How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?
reflection: Hebrews compares the old sacrifices with the sacrifice of Jesus: "How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?" Many people serve out of guilt, trying to earn forgiveness or quiet an accusing conscience. These are dead works, efforts that cannot bring life. But the blood of Christ cleanses our consciences. When we know we are forgiven, we are freed to serve God not out of fear, but out of gratitude and love. Service becomes a joyful response rather than a desperate attempt. Notice the phrase the living God. We serve a God who is alive, who sees us, and who delights in our service. Today, if guilt has been driving your service, bring it to the cross. Let the blood of Christ cleanse your conscience. Then serve the living God freely, with a willing heart.
question: Has guilt been driving your service, and how can you let Christ cleanse your conscience?
prayer: Lord Jesus, Your blood purges my conscience from dead works. Free me from serving out of guilt, and let me serve the living God with a willing heart. Amen.

text: Who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.
reflection: Paul describes himself and his co-workers as ministers of a new covenant: "Who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life." Notice that God made them able. Their ability to serve came from God, not from themselves. And the service they offered was life-giving. The letter, the law written on stone, could show people their sin, but it could not give them power to change. The Spirit, however, writes God's law on hearts and brings new life. This shapes how we serve others. Service that only focuses on rules and requirements can crush people. Service filled with the Spirit brings life, hope, and freedom. When we serve, we are not merely enforcing standards. We are pointing people to the life-giving grace of God. Today, ask God to make you an able minister. Serve in a way that gives life to those around you.
question: How could you serve in a way that gives life to those around you today?
prayer: Lord, make me an able minister of the new covenant. Help me serve in a way that points people to Your life-giving grace and not only to rules. Amen.

text: And ofttimes it hath cast him into the fire, and into the waters, to destroy him: but if thou canst do any thing, have compassion on us, and help us.
reflection: A desperate father brought his son to Jesus. For years the boy had suffered terribly. The father pleaded, "but if thou canst do any thing, have compassion on us, and help us." His faith was weak. He was not even sure Jesus could help. But he asked for compassion. And Jesus responded. He gently challenged the father's faith, and the father cried out, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Jesus healed the boy. This story is a comfort for anyone whose faith feels shaky. You do not need perfect faith to come to Jesus. You can come with your doubts and your desperation. You can simply ask for compassion. And Jesus will meet you there. Having received such mercy, we are called to extend it. When others come to us struggling and uncertain, we can respond with compassion rather than judgment. Today, bring your honest need to Jesus. And show compassion to someone else who is struggling to believe.
question: What honest need can you bring to Jesus today, even with uncertain faith?
prayer: Lord, I believe; help my unbelief. Have compassion on me in my need, and make me compassionate toward others who are struggling to believe. Amen.

text: Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name…
reflection: Paul describes the humility of Jesus, who emptied Himself, became a servant, and died on the cross. Then comes the turning point: "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name." Jesus gave Himself completely, and God responded by giving Him the highest honor. The way down became the way up. This reveals something about God's generosity. He honors those who give themselves for others. Jesus gave His life, and the Father gave Him a name above every name. One day, every knee will bow at the name of Jesus. Our own giving, though small in comparison, is part of this same pattern. When we give generously and serve humbly, we follow the path of Jesus. And God sees. He is not indifferent to sacrifice. Today, honor the name of Jesus with your words and actions. And follow His example of humble, generous self-giving, trusting God to honor what is done in love.
question: How can you honor the name of Jesus with your words and actions today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, Your name is above every name. Help me honor You today, and follow Your example of humble, generous self-giving. Amen.

text: But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
reflection: James writes, "But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble." What a wonderful phrase: He giveth more grace. Whatever we face, God's grace is greater. When temptation is strong, He gives more grace. When we fail again, He gives more grace. When the burden is heavy, He gives more grace. But this grace flows to the humble. Pride resists God's help. It insists on doing things its own way. Humility opens the door. It admits need and receives what God gives freely. This is why serving others with humility is so powerful. It keeps our hearts in a posture to receive grace. Today, wherever you feel stretched beyond your ability, humble yourself before God. Admit your need. Ask for His help. And trust that His grace will meet you. He always has more to give. His supply never runs dry.
question: Where do you feel stretched beyond your ability, and can you humbly ask God for more grace?
prayer: Lord, You give more grace. I humble myself before You and admit my need. Meet me with Your grace, which never runs dry. Amen.

text: All my state shall Tychicus declare unto you, who is a beloved brother, and a faithful minister and fellowservant in the Lord…
reflection: Paul introduces a co-worker named Tychicus with three warm descriptions: "a beloved brother, and a faithful minister and fellowservant in the Lord." Tychicus is not one of the famous names in the Bible. He was a messenger who carried letters and news between Paul and the churches. Yet Paul honored him as beloved, faithful, and a fellow servant. This is love expressed in action. Tychicus served behind the scenes, traveling long distances to deliver encouragement. His work was practical and often unseen, but it mattered deeply. Many of the most important acts of love happen quietly. A parent caring for a child, a friend driving someone to an appointment, a volunteer setting up chairs, a messenger delivering encouragement. God sees these faithful servants and calls them beloved. Today, honor someone who serves faithfully behind the scenes. Thank them for their work. And if you are serving quietly yourself, take heart. You are beloved and faithful in God's eyes.
question: Who serves faithfully behind the scenes whom you could thank today?
prayer: Lord, thank You for the faithful people who serve quietly behind the scenes. Help me honor them, and make me beloved and faithful in my own quiet service. Amen.

text: Is the law then against the promises of God? God forbid: for if there had been a law given which could have given life, verily righteousness should have been by the law.
reflection: Paul asks a question: "Is the law then against the promises of God? God forbid." The law is good. It reveals God's holiness. But it was never meant to give life. Paul explains, "if there had been a law given which could have given life, verily righteousness should have been by the law." No law, no set of rules, no amount of effort can make us right with God. Only God's promise, fulfilled in Jesus and received by faith, can do that. This is freeing. We can stop trying to earn righteousness through our performance. We are made right by grace. But it is also a calling. Once we are made right, God calls us to live rightly, not to earn His love but to reflect it. Righteousness becomes the fruit of grace rather than its root. Today, rest in the righteousness God has given you through Christ. And let it overflow into right living: treating others fairly, speaking truth, and doing good.
question: How can the righteousness God has given you overflow into right living today?
prayer: Lord, no law could give me life, but You have made me right through Christ. Let Your gift of righteousness overflow into fairness, truth, and good works today. Amen.

text: He therefore that despiseth, despiseth not man, but God, who hath also given unto us his holy Spirit.
reflection: Paul reminds the Thessalonians of something precious: God "hath also given unto us his holy Spirit." The Spirit is God's gift, the presence of God Himself living within us. Paul had just urged them to live in holiness, and he warns that whoever rejects this call rejects not a human teacher, but God. Why does it matter so much? Because God has given us His Spirit. Living in a way that dishonors Him is like treating a priceless gift carelessly. But honoring His gift is a joy. The Spirit helps us live in purity, love, and generosity. As this month of service and compassion ends, remember the greatest gift you have been given. God did not hold back His own presence. He gave Himself to dwell in you. Let that generosity shape your life. Honor His gift by living for Him, and share His love freely with everyone you meet. Every act of compassion becomes a way of honoring the Spirit within you.
question: How can you honor the gift of the Holy Spirit by the way you live and love today?
prayer: Father, thank You for giving me Your Holy Spirit. Help me honor that gift by living for You and sharing Your love freely with everyone I meet. Amen.
